concepts: Non-trivial solution of a homogeneous linear system
questions.question: If the equations $a(y+z)=x$, $b(z+x)=y$, $c(x+y)=z$ have nontrivial solutions, then find the value of $\frac{1}{1+a}+\frac{1}{1+b}+\frac{1}{1+c}$.
questions.key_idea: A homogeneous system has a non-trivial solution exactly when its determinant is $0$; one column operation then makes it factorise.
solution: Write the system in homogeneous form: $x-ay-az=0$, $bx-y+bz=0$, $cx+cy-z=0$.
A non-trivial solution exists only if $D=\begin{vmatrix} 1 & -a & -a \\ b & -1 & b \\ c & c & -1 \end{vmatrix}=0$.
Apply $C_1\to C_1-C_2$ and $C_2\to C_2-C_3$: $\begin{vmatrix} 1+a & 0 & -a \\ b+1 & -(1+b) & b \\ 0 & c+1 & -1 \end{vmatrix}=0$.
Expand along the first column: $(1+a)\left[(1+b)-b(c+1)\right]-(1+b)\,a(c+1)=0$.
Since $\frac{b}{1+b}=1-\frac{1}{1+b}$ and $\frac{a}{1+a}=1-\frac{1}{1+a}$, this gives $\frac{1}{1+c}+\frac{1}{1+b}+\frac{1}{1+a}=2$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF labels the step only as $C_1\to C_1-C_2$, but the determinant it prints needs both $C_1\to C_1-C_2$ and $C_2\to C_2-C_3$ (second column $0,-(1+b),c+1$); both operations are now named. Rest of the working and the answer 2 are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Add the three equations: with $s=x+y+z$ each equation reads $x=\frac{a\,s}{1+a}$, so summing gives the answer at once.
solution: Let $s=x+y+z$. Then $y+z=s-x$, so the first equation is $a(s-x)=x$, i.e. $x=\frac{a\,s}{1+a}$; similarly $y=\frac{b\,s}{1+b}$, $z=\frac{c\,s}{1+c}$.
If $s=0$ then $(1+a)x=0$, $(1+b)y=0$, $(1+c)z=0$ and (as $1+a,1+b,1+c\neq0$) $x=y=z=0$, which is trivial. So $s\neq0$.
Add the three expressions: $s=s\left(\frac{a}{1+a}+\frac{b}{1+b}+\frac{c}{1+c}\right)$; cancel $s\neq0$.
Hence $\sum\frac{a}{1+a}=1$, i.e. $\sum\left(1-\frac{1}{1+a}\right)=1$, so $3-\sum\frac{1}{1+a}=1$.
Therefore $\frac{1}{1+a}+\frac{1}{1+b}+\frac{1}{1+c}=2$ (no determinant needed).

useful_results: A homogeneous system $AX=0$ has a non-trivial solution if and only if $\det A=0$.
Symmetric systems such as $a(y+z)=x$: put $s=x+y+z$, so $y+z=s-x$ and each variable becomes $\frac{a s}{1+a}$.
The condition is equivalent to $\sum\frac{1}{1+a}=2$ and also to $ab+bc+ca+2abc=1$ (check $a=b=c=\frac12$: $\frac34+\frac14=1$).
Column operations $C_i\to C_i-C_j$ are the quickest way to create zeros in such determinants.

concepts: Non-trivial solution of a homogeneous linear system
questions.question: Given $a=\frac{x}{y-z}$, $b=\frac{y}{z-x}$, $c=\frac{z}{x-y}$ where $x,y,z$ are not all zero, prove that $1+ab+bc+ca=0$.
questions.key_idea: Cleared of denominators the three relations form a homogeneous system in $x,y,z$ with a non-zero solution, so its determinant vanishes.
solution: From the definitions: $ay-az=x$, $bz-bx=y$, $cx-cy=z$.
Rewrite as a homogeneous system: $x-ay+az=0$, $bx+y-bz=0$, $cx-cy-z=0$.
As $x,y,z$ are not all zero, the determinant must vanish: $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & -a & a \\ b & 1 & -b \\ c & -c & -1 \end{vmatrix}=0$.
Expand along the first row: $(-1-bc)+a(-b+bc)+a(-bc-c)=0$.
Simplify: $-1-bc-ab+abc-abc-ac=0$.
Hence $1+ab+bc+ca=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $p=y-z$, $q=z-x$, $r=x-y$ (so $p+q+r=0$) and use the cyclic identity $xy(x-y)+yz(y-z)+zx(z-x)=-(x-y)(y-z)(z-x)$.
solution: With $p=y-z$, $q=z-x$, $r=x-y$ we have $a=\frac{x}{p}$, $b=\frac{y}{q}$, $c=\frac{z}{r}$.
Then $ab+bc+ca=\frac{xy}{pq}+\frac{yz}{qr}+\frac{zx}{rp}=\frac{xy\,r+yz\,p+zx\,q}{pqr}$.
The numerator is $xy(x-y)+yz(y-z)+zx(z-x)$.
This cyclic sum equals $-(x-y)(y-z)(z-x)=-rpq$ (check $x=0$: $yz(y-z)$ on the left; on the right $-(-y)(y-z)(z)=yz(y-z)$).
So $ab+bc+ca=\frac{-pqr}{pqr}=-1$, i.e. $1+ab+bc+ca=0$.

useful_results: Cyclic identity: $xy(x-y)+yz(y-z)+zx(z-x)=-(x-y)(y-z)(z-x)$ (it vanishes when any two variables are equal).
If $a=\frac{x}{y-z}$, $b=\frac{y}{z-x}$, $c=\frac{z}{x-y}$ then $ab+bc+ca=-1$, so $(a+b+c)^2=a^2+b^2+c^2-2$.
Any relation that is homogeneous and linear in $x,y,z$ with a common non-zero solution forces the coefficient determinant to be $0$.

concepts: Solving a system of linear equations by elimination
Compound-angle formulae
questions.question: If $\sin q\neq\cos q$ and $x,y,z$ satisfy the equations $x\cos p-y\sin p+z=\cos q+1$, $x\sin p+y\cos p+z=1-\sin q$, $x\cos(p+q)-y\sin(p+q)+z=2$, then find the value of $x^2+y^2+z^2$.
questions.key_idea: Combine the first two equations with weights $\cos q$ and $-\sin q$ to build the left side of the third; $z$ drops out as $z=1$.
solution: Label: (1) $x\cos p-y\sin p+z=\cos q+1$, (2) $x\sin p+y\cos p+z=1-\sin q$, (4) $x\cos(p+q)-y\sin(p+q)+z=2$.
Multiply (1) by $\cos q$ and (2) by $\sin q$ and subtract: (3) $x\cos(p+q)-y\sin(p+q)+z(\cos q-\sin q)=1+\cos q-\sin q$ (using $\cos^2q+\sin^2q=1$).
Subtract (4) from (3): $z(\cos q-\sin q-1)=\cos q-\sin q-1$.
Cancelling the factor $\cos q-\sin q-1$ (assumed non-zero) gives $z=1$.
Put $z=1$ in (1) and (2): $x\cos p-y\sin p=\cos q$ and $x\sin p+y\cos p=-\sin q$.
Multiply the first by $\cos p$ and the second by $\sin p$ and add: $x=\cos p\cos q-\sin p\sin q=\cos(p+q)$.
Multiply the first by $-\sin p$ and the second by $\cos p$ and add: $y=-\sin p\cos q-\cos p\sin q=-\sin(p+q)$.
questions.correction_note: Two defects in the PDF: (i) the line 'x cos p + y sin p = cos q' should read 'x cos p − y sin p = cos q' (sign slip; the later results are right); (ii) cancelling cos q − sin q − 1 needs cos q − sin q ≠ 1, which the stated condition sin q ≠ cos q does not give (at q = 0 equations 1 and 3 coincide and x²+y²+z² is not fixed). The key 2 holds under this extra assumption, now stated.

alternate_solutions.idea: Guess the solution $x=\cos(p+q)$, $y=-\sin(p+q)$, $z=1$, check it in all three equations, and use a non-zero coefficient determinant for uniqueness.
solution: Coefficient determinant: $\Delta=\begin{vmatrix} \cos p & -\sin p & 1 \\ \sin p & \cos p & 1 \\ \cos(p+q) & -\sin(p+q) & 1 \end{vmatrix}=1-\cos q+\sin q$.
So $\Delta\neq0$ whenever $\cos q-\sin q\neq1$, and then the system has exactly one solution.
Try $x=\cos(p+q)$, $y=-\sin(p+q)$, $z=1$. Equation 1: $\cos(p+q)\cos p+\sin(p+q)\sin p+1=\cos q+1$ ✓.
Equation 2: $\cos(p+q)\sin p-\sin(p+q)\cos p+1=-\sin q+1$ ✓. Equation 3: $\cos^2(p+q)+\sin^2(p+q)+1=2$ ✓.
By uniqueness this is the solution, so $x^2+y^2+z^2=1+1=2$.

useful_results: $x\cos\theta-y\sin\theta$ and $x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta$ are the coordinates of $(x,y)$ rotated by $\theta$, so $\left(x\cos\theta-y\sin\theta\right)^2+\left(x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta\right)^2=x^2+y^2$.
In complex form: $(x+iy)e^{i\theta}=(x\cos\theta-y\sin\theta)+i(x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta)$.
A linear system with $\det\neq0$ has exactly one solution, so a guessed triple that satisfies all equations is the solution (guess and verify).
Here the coefficient determinant is $1-(\cos q-\sin q)$; it vanishes at $q=0$, where equations 1 and 3 coincide.

concepts: Consistency of a system of linear equations (unique, infinite, no solution)
questions.question: Investigate for what values of $\lambda,\mu$ the simultaneous equations $x+y+z=6$; $x+2y+3z=10$ and $x+2y+\lambda z=\mu$ have: (a) a unique solution, (b) an infinite number of solutions, (c) no solution.
questions.key_idea: Subtracting the second equation from the third leaves $(\lambda-3)z=\mu-10$, which decides all three cases.
solution: The PDF's working printed under this question belongs to Q5 (a system in $k$), so the solution is written here from the question.
Subtract equation 1 from equation 2: $y+2z=4$.
Subtract equation 2 from equation 3: $(\lambda-3)z=\mu-10$.
The system is equivalent to $x+y+z=6$, $y+2z=4$, $(\lambda-3)z=\mu-10$.
(a) If $\lambda\neq3$: $z=\frac{\mu-10}{\lambda-3}$ is determined, then $y$ and $x$ follow: a unique solution for every $\mu$. (Equivalently $D=\lambda-3\neq0$.)
(b) If $\lambda=3$ and $\mu=10$: the last equation is $0=0$, leaving two equations in three unknowns. Put $z=t$: $y=4-2t$, $x=2+t$, infinitely many solutions.
(c) If $\lambda=3$ and $\mu\neq10$: the last equation reads $0=\mu-10\neq0$, which is impossible, so there is no solution.
questions.correction_note: The solution printed in the PDF under Q4 is the solution of Q5 (the system with parameter k and the unknown determinant 2(k-2)(k^2+2k+15)); it does not answer Q4. A fresh solution was written; the printed answers (a) λ≠3, (b) λ=3 μ=10, (c) λ=3 μ≠10 are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use Cramer's rule: $D=\lambda-3$, $D_3=\mu-10$, and classify by the values of the determinants.
solution: $D=\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & \lambda \end{vmatrix}=(2\lambda-6)-(\lambda-3)+0=\lambda-3$.

$D_1=\begin{vmatrix} 6 & 1 & 1 \\ 10 & 2 & 3 \\ \mu & 2 & \lambda \end{vmatrix}=2\lambda+\mu-16$, $D_2=\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 6 & 1 \\ 1 & 10 & 3 \\ 1 & \mu & \lambda \end{vmatrix}=4\lambda-2\mu+8$, $D_3=\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 1 & 2 & 10 \\ 1 & 2 & \mu \end{vmatrix}=\mu-10$.
(a) $D\neq0\iff\lambda\neq3$: a unique solution.
(c) $\lambda=3$ gives $D=0$; if $\mu\neq10$ then $D_3\neq0$, so the system is inconsistent: no solution.
(b) $\lambda=3$, $\mu=10$: $D=D_1=D_2=D_3=0$, and the first two equations are independent (rank $2$) and consistent, so the solutions form a line: infinitely many.

useful_results: For $AX=B$ with $\det A=D$: $D\neq0$ gives a unique solution; $D=0$ with some $D_i\neq0$ gives no solution.
$D=D_1=D_2=D_3=0$ is only necessary for infinitely many solutions: planes can still be parallel, so check consistency (rank of $A$ = rank of $[A|B]$).
When two equations differ only in one coefficient and the constant, subtract them: the result $(\lambda-3)z=\mu-10$ is the whole classification.
For $x+y+z=6$, $x+2y+3z=10$ the solutions with $\lambda=3,\mu=10$ are $(2+t,\,4-2t,\,t)$.

concepts: Cramer's rule for a parametric 3×3 system
questions.question: Solve the equations $Kx+2y-2z=1$, $4x+2Ky-z=2$, $6x+6y+Kz=3$, considering specially the case $K=2$. If $K=2$, then $x=\lambda$, $y=\frac{1-2\lambda}{2}$ and $z=0$, where $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$.
questions.key_idea: Cramer's rule: $D=2(K-2)(K^2+2K+15)$ vanishes only at $K=2$ because the quadratic factor has negative discriminant.
solution: For a unique solution $K\neq2$ (the quadratic $K^2+2K+15$ has no real root).
If $K=2$ then $D=D_1=D_2=D_3=0$. The equations become $2x+2y-2z=1$, $4x+4y-z=2$, $6x+6y+2z=3$; with $x+y=s$: $s-z=\frac12$, $4s-z=2$ give $s=\frac12$, $z=0$, and $6s+2z=3$ holds.
So the system is consistent with infinitely many solutions: $x=\lambda$, $y=\frac{1-2\lambda}{2}$, $z=0$, $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$.
questions.correction_note: Gap, not a wrong value: the PDF just says 'If k = 2, infinite solution; put x = λ' without showing that the system is consistent at k = 2 (needed for infinitely many solutions). The check (x+y=1/2, z=0 satisfying all three equations) was added. All determinants, solutions and the key are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate $y$ without determinants: eq3 $-\,3\times$ eq1 and eq2 $-\,K\times$ eq1 both involve only $x$ and $z$, and the factor $(2-K)$ appears by itself.
solution: Equation 3 $-\,3\times$ equation 1: $(6-3K)x+(K+6)z=0$, so $(K+6)z=3(K-2)x$.
Equation 2 $-\,K\times$ equation 1: $(4-K^2)x+(2K-1)z=2-K$, i.e. $(2-K)(2+K)x+(2K-1)z=2-K$.
For $K\neq2$ substitute $z=\frac{3(K-2)x}{K+6}$ and divide by $(2-K)$: $x\left[(2+K)-\frac{3(2K-1)}{K+6}\right]=1$.
Then $z=\frac{3(K-2)}{K^2+2K+15}$ and $y$ from equation 1: $y=\frac{1-Kx+2z}{2}=\frac{2K+3}{2(K^2+2K+15)}$.
For $K=2$ both combinations give $8z=0$ and $3z=0$, so $z=0$ and the equations collapse to $x+y=\frac12$: $x=\lambda$, $y=\frac{1-2\lambda}{2}$.

useful_results: Cramer's rule is clean when the determinants factor: look for the factor that makes $D=0$ and test whether the other factors are positive or have no real roots.
A quadratic factor such as $K^2+2K+15$ has discriminant $4-60<0$, so it never vanishes for real $K$.
Spot proportional coefficients: here the $y$-coefficients $2,\,2K,\,6$ let eq3 $-\,3\,$eq1 remove $y$ immediately.
At the singular value ($D=0$) always finish with a consistency check by elimination: $D=D_i=0$ alone does not prove infinitely many solutions.

concepts: Cramer's rule for a 2×2 system
Selection of distinct numbers and optimisation
questions.question: Let $a,b,c,d$ be distinct numbers chosen from the set $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$. If the least possible positive solution for $x$ to the system $ax+by=1$, $cx+dy=2$ can be expressed in the form $\frac{p}{q}$ where $p$ and $q$ are relatively prime, then find the value of $(p+q)$.
questions.key_idea: By Cramer's rule $x=\frac{d-2b}{ad-bc}$; a small positive numerator over the largest possible denominator gives the least value.
solution: By Cramer's rule $x=\frac{D_1}{D}=\frac{\begin{vmatrix} 1 & b \\ 2 & d \end{vmatrix}}{\begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix}}=\frac{d-2b}{ad-bc}$.
To get the least positive value, $d-2b$ must be as small as possible and $ad-bc$ as large as possible. Take $d-2b=1$.
Case I: $d=5,\ b=2$. Then $x=\frac{1}{5a-2c}$ with $a,c\in\{1,3,4\}$; $5a-2c$ is largest for $a=4,\ c=1$, giving $x=\frac{1}{18}$.
Case II: $d=3,\ b=1$. Then $x=\frac{1}{3a-c}$ with $a,c\in\{2,4,5\}$; $3a-c$ is largest for $a=5,\ c=2$, giving $x=\frac{1}{13}$.
Since $\frac{1}{18}<\frac{1}{13}$, the smaller is $\frac{1}{18}$.
Other numerators cannot do better: if $|d-2b|\ge2$ then $x\ge\frac{2}{18}$, because $|ad-bc|\le5\cdot4-1\cdot2=18$.
If $d-2b=-1$ (so $(b,d)=(2,3)$ or $(3,5)$) we need $ad-bc<0$; the largest $|ad-bc|$ is only $7$, giving $x=\frac17>\frac1{18}$.
So the least positive value is $x=\frac{1}{18}$, hence $p=1,\ q=18$ and $p+q=19$.
questions.correction_note: Gap: the PDF only examines numerator d−2b = +1 and never shows that numerators ≥ 2 or the negative numerator d−2b = −1 (with ad−bc<0) cannot give a smaller positive x. Both cases were added (largest |ad−bc| is 18, resp. 7). Answer 19 confirmed by brute force over all 120 choices.

alternate_solutions.idea: The numerator is a positive integer and $|ad-bc|\le18$, so $x\ge\frac1{18}$; then exhibit a choice that attains it.
solution: $x=\frac{d-2b}{ad-bc}$. A positive $x$ has numerator and denominator of the same sign, so $x\ge\frac{1}{|ad-bc|}$ because $|d-2b|\ge1$ is an integer.
For distinct numbers from $\{1,\dots,5\}$: $ad-bc\le5\cdot4-1\cdot2=18$ and $bc-ad\le5\cdot4-1\cdot2=18$, so $|ad-bc|\le18$.
Hence $x\ge\frac1{18}$ for every admissible choice.
Equality needs numerator $1$ and $|ad-bc|=18$: take $a=4,\ b=2,\ c=1,\ d=5$: $d-2b=1$ and $ad-bc=20-2=18$, so $x=\frac1{18}$.
So the least value is $\frac1{18}$ and $p+q=19$.

useful_results: For a ratio of integers, a positive value is at least $\frac{1}{\text{largest possible denominator}}$; then show that the bound is attained.
For distinct entries from $\{1,\dots,n\}$: $|ad-bc|\le n(n-1)-1\cdot2$ (largest product pair minus smallest product pair).
2×2 Cramer's rule: for $ax+by=e$, $cx+dy=f$: $x=\frac{ed-bf}{ad-bc}$, $y=\frac{af-ec}{ad-bc}$.
Brute force over all $5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2=120$ ordered choices confirms the minimum $\frac{1}{18}$ attained at $(a,b,c,d)=(4,2,1,5)$.

concepts: Consistency and solution set of a parametric linear system
questions.question: Show that the system of equations $3x-y+4z=3$, $x+2y-3z=-2$ and $6x+5y+\lambda z=-3$ has at least one solution for any real number $\lambda$. Find the set of solutions for $\lambda=-5$.
questions.answer: At least one solution for every $\lambda$ (unique $\left(\frac47,-\frac97,0\right)$ if $\lambda\neq-5$); for $\lambda=-5$: $x=\frac{4-5K}{7}$, $y=\frac{13K-9}{7}$, $z=K$, $K\in\mathbb{R}$
questions.key_idea: The determinant is $7(\lambda+5)$; at $\lambda=-5$ put $z=K$, solve two equations and check the third.
solution: $D=\begin{vmatrix} 3 & -1 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 6 & 5 & \lambda \end{vmatrix}=3(2\lambda+15)+(\lambda+18)+4(5-12)=7\lambda+35=7(\lambda+5)$.
If $\lambda\neq-5$ then $D\neq0$, so the system has a unique solution; thus at least one solution exists.
For $\lambda=-5$ put $z=k$: $3x-y=3-4k$ (1) and $x+2y=-2+3k$ (2).
Multiply (1) by $2$ and add (2): $7x=6-8k-2+3k=4-5k$, so $x=\frac{4-5k}{7}$.
Check the third equation $6x+5y-5z=-3$: $\frac{6(4-5k)+5(13k-9)-35k}{7}=\frac{-21}{7}=-3$ ✓, so it holds for every $k$.
Hence for $\lambda=-5$ the solution set is $\left\{\left(\frac{4-5k}{7},\frac{13k-9}{7},k\right):k\in\mathbb{R}\right\}$ (infinitely many).
questions.correction_note: Three fixes: (i) the PDF says 'multiply eq. (1) by 2 and subtract eq. (2)' but its next line (7x = 4 − 5k) is obtained by adding; (ii) it never checks that the third equation holds at λ = −5 (needed for 'at least one solution'); (iii) the printed key reads 'If λ = 5' where λ = −5 is meant (for λ ≠ −5 the unique solution is (4/7, −9/7, 0)). Final solution set is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Set $z=0$: the unknown parameter $\lambda$ disappears, and the first two equations already give a solution of the third for every $\lambda$.
solution: With $z=0$ the first two equations are $3x-y=3$, $x+2y=-2$; add twice the first to the second: $7x=4$, so $x=\frac47$, $y=-\frac97$.
Third equation: $6\cdot\frac47+5\left(-\frac97\right)+\lambda\cdot0=\frac{24-45}{7}=-3$ ✓ for every $\lambda$.
So $\left(\frac47,-\frac97,0\right)$ is a solution for every real $\lambda$: at least one solution always exists.
For $\lambda=-5$ the rows $(3,-1,4)$ and $(1,2,-3)$ give the direction $(3,-1,4)\times(1,2,-3)=(-5,13,7)$, and $(6,5,-5)\cdot(-5,13,7)=0$, so the third plane contains this direction.
Therefore the solution set is the line $\left(\frac47,-\frac97,0\right)+t(-5,13,7)$; with $z=7t=K$ this is $\left(\frac{4-5K}{7},\frac{13K-9}{7},K\right)$.

useful_results: If the parameter multiplies only one variable, try that variable $=0$: the parameter-free solution then works for all values.
When $\operatorname{rank}A=2$ in $3\times3$ and the system is consistent, the solutions form a line: a particular solution plus $t\,(\mathbf r_1\times\mathbf r_2)$.
$D=0$ does not show consistency; check that the dependent equation is satisfied (here $-21/7=-3$).
The cross product of two rows gives the direction vector of the null space when the third row is a combination of them.

concepts: Cramer's rule with Vandermonde-type determinants
questions.question: Solve the system of equations $z+ay+a^2x+a^3=0$, $z+by+b^2x+b^3=0$, $z+cy+c^2x+c^3=0$.
questions.key_idea: The determinants are Vandermonde-type: the common factor $(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$ cancels from every ratio.
solution: Write the system as $a^2x+ay+z=-a^3$, $b^2x+by+z=-b^3$, $c^2x+cy+z=-c^3$ (take $a,b,c$ distinct).
$D=\begin{vmatrix} a^2 & a & 1 \\ b^2 & b & 1 \\ c^2 & c & 1 \end{vmatrix}=-(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)\neq0$.
$D_1=\begin{vmatrix} -a^3 & a & 1 \\ -b^3 & b & 1 \\ -c^3 & c & 1 \end{vmatrix}=(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)(a+b+c)$.
$D_2=\begin{vmatrix} a^2 & -a^3 & 1 \\ b^2 & -b^3 & 1 \\ c^2 & -c^3 & 1 \end{vmatrix}=-(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)(ab+bc+ca)$.
$D_3=\begin{vmatrix} a^2 & a & -a^3 \\ b^2 & b & -b^3 \\ c^2 & c & -c^3 \end{vmatrix}=abc\,(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$.
$y=\frac{D_2}{D}=ab+bc+ca$.
$z=\frac{D_3}{D}=-abc$.
questions.correction_note: Sign errors in the PDF: it gives D = (a−b)(b−c)(c−a), but the determinant equals −(a−b)(b−c)(c−a); its D1 and D3 also carry the wrong sign (D1 = +(a−b)(b−c)(c−a)(a+b+c), D3 = +abc(a−b)(b−c)(c−a)), while D2 is right. With the PDF's D the ratio for y comes out −(ab+bc+ca), contradicting the PDF's own key. Corrected values give x, y, z as in the key.

alternate_solutions.idea: Read the equations as $t^3+xt^2+yt+z=0$ at $t=a,b,c$: so $a,b,c$ are the three roots of a monic cubic, and Vieta's formulas give $x,y,z$ immediately.
solution: Each equation says $t^3+xt^2+yt+z=0$ holds for $t=a$, $t=b$ and $t=c$.
For distinct $a,b,c$ the monic cubic with these three roots is unique: $t^3+xt^2+yt+z=(t-a)(t-b)(t-c)$.
Expand: $(t-a)(t-b)(t-c)=t^3-(a+b+c)t^2+(ab+bc+ca)t-abc$.
Compare coefficients: $x=-(a+b+c)$, $y=ab+bc+ca$, $z=-abc$.

useful_results: Vandermonde: $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 1 & b & b^2 \\ 1 & c & c^2 \end{vmatrix}=(b-a)(c-a)(c-b)$; interchanging two columns changes the sign (here $D=(a-b)(a-c)(b-c)$).
A system $f(t_i)=0$ for a polynomial with unknown coefficients is an interpolation problem; Vieta's relations give the coefficients at once.

Generalised Vandermonde: $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & a^2 & a^3 \\ 1 & b^2 & b^3 \\ 1 & c^2 & c^3 \end{vmatrix}=(ab+bc+ca)\cdot\begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 1 & b & b^2 \\ 1 & c & c^2 \end{vmatrix}$ (power sums become elementary symmetric functions).
Distinctness of $a,b,c$ is needed: otherwise $D=0$ and the solution is not unique.

concepts: Properties of determinants (scalar multiples and row/column operations)
questions.question: If $a^2+b^2+c^2=1$ then show that the value of the determinant $\begin{vmatrix} a^2+(b^2+c^2)\cos\theta & ab(1-\cos\theta) & ac(1-\cos\theta) \\ ba(1-\cos\theta) & b^2+(c^2+a^2)\cos\theta & bc(1-\cos\theta) \\ ca(1-\cos\theta) & cb(1-\cos\theta) & c^2+(a^2+b^2)\cos\theta \end{vmatrix}$ simplifies to $\cos^2\theta$.
questions.key_idea: Multiply the columns by $a,b,c$ and take $a,b,c$ out of the rows to get squares; then $C_1\to C_1+C_2+C_3$ makes the first column all equal to $a^2+b^2+c^2$.
solution: Let $\Delta$ be the determinant and $s=a^2+b^2+c^2$ (so $s=1$ at the end); take $abc\neq0$.
Multiply $C_1,C_2,C_3$ by $a,b,c$ and divide by $abc$; then take $a,b,c$ out of $R_1,R_2,R_3$ (this multiplies by $abc$ and cancels the division). The squares appear:

$\Delta=\begin{vmatrix} a^2+(b^2+c^2)\cos\theta & b^2(1-\cos\theta) & c^2(1-\cos\theta) \\ a^2(1-\cos\theta) & b^2+(c^2+a^2)\cos\theta & c^2(1-\cos\theta) \\ a^2(1-\cos\theta) & b^2(1-\cos\theta) & c^2+(a^2+b^2)\cos\theta \end{vmatrix}$.

Apply $C_1\to C_1+C_2+C_3$: every entry of the new first column is $a^2+b^2+c^2=s$ (the $\cos\theta$ terms cancel). Take $s$ out: $\Delta=s\begin{vmatrix} 1 & b^2(1-\cos\theta) & c^2(1-\cos\theta) \\ 1 & b^2+(c^2+a^2)\cos\theta & c^2(1-\cos\theta) \\ 1 & b^2(1-\cos\theta) & c^2+(a^2+b^2)\cos\theta \end{vmatrix}$.
Apply $R_2\to R_2-R_1$ and $R_3\to R_3-R_1$: $\Delta=s\begin{vmatrix} 1 & b^2(1-\cos\theta) & c^2(1-\cos\theta) \\ 0 & s\cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & s\cos\theta \end{vmatrix}$.
Expand: $\Delta=s\cdot(s\cos\theta)^2=s^3\cos^2\theta$.
With $a^2+b^2+c^2=1$: $\Delta=\cos^2\theta$, independent of $a,b,c$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The matrix is $s\cos\theta\,I+(1-\cos\theta)\,\mathbf v\mathbf v^{T}$ with $\mathbf v=(a,b,c)^T$; a rank-one update of a scalar matrix has eigenvalues $s\cos\theta$ (twice) and $s$.
solution: Entry check: diagonal $a^2+(b^2+c^2)\cos\theta=a^2(1-\cos\theta)+s\cos\theta$; off-diagonal $ab(1-\cos\theta)$.
Hence $M=s\cos\theta\,I+(1-\cos\theta)\,\mathbf v\mathbf v^{T}$, where $\mathbf v^T\mathbf v=a^2+b^2+c^2=s$.
On vectors orthogonal to $\mathbf v$ (a $2$-dimensional space) $M$ acts as multiplication by $s\cos\theta$.
On $\mathbf v$: $M\mathbf v=s\cos\theta\,\mathbf v+(1-\cos\theta)s\,\mathbf v=s\,\mathbf v$.
So $\det M=s\cdot(s\cos\theta)^2=s^3\cos^2\theta=\cos^2\theta$ for $s=1$.

useful_results: Matrix determinant lemma: $\det(\lambda I+\mathbf u\mathbf v^T)=\lambda^{n-1}(\lambda+\mathbf v^T\mathbf u)$.
Pattern: entries $a_ia_j\,k$ off the diagonal with diagonal $a_i^2k+m$ mean a rank-one matrix plus a scalar matrix.
Check: $\theta=0$ gives $M=s\,I$ and $\det=s^3$; $\theta=\pi/2$ gives $M=\mathbf v\mathbf v^T$ (rank $1$) and $\det=0=\cos^2\frac\pi2$.
A column operation that adds all columns is the first thing to try when every row sums to the same value.

concepts: Evaluating determinants by column operations
Half-angle ratios tan and cot in a triangle
questions.question: In a $\triangle ABC$, determine the condition under which $\begin{vmatrix} \cot\frac A2 & \cot\frac B2 & \cot\frac C2 \\ \tan\frac B2+\tan\frac C2 & \tan\frac C2+\tan\frac A2 & \tan\frac A2+\tan\frac B2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}=0$.
questions.key_idea: Differences of columns turn the third row into $(0,0,1)$ and the tangent differences become cotangent differences, exposing a product of three differences.
solution: Apply $C_1\to C_1-C_2$ and $C_2\to C_2-C_3$: $\begin{vmatrix} \cot\frac A2-\cot\frac B2 & \cot\frac B2-\cot\frac C2 & \cot\frac C2 \\ \tan\frac B2-\tan\frac A2 & \tan\frac C2-\tan\frac B2 & \tan\frac A2+\tan\frac B2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix}=0$.
Use $\tan\frac B2-\tan\frac A2=\frac{1}{\cot\frac B2}-\frac{1}{\cot\frac A2}=\frac{\cot\frac A2-\cot\frac B2}{\cot\frac A2\cot\frac B2}$.
Similarly $\tan\frac C2-\tan\frac B2=\frac{\cot\frac B2-\cot\frac C2}{\cot\frac B2\cot\frac C2}$.

Take the common factors $\left(\cot\frac A2-\cot\frac B2\right)$ out of $C_1$ and $\left(\cot\frac B2-\cot\frac C2\right)$ out of $C_2$: $\left(\cot\frac A2-\cot\frac B2\right)\left(\cot\frac B2-\cot\frac C2\right)\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & \cot\frac C2 \\ \frac{1}{\cot\frac A2\cot\frac B2} & \frac{1}{\cot\frac B2\cot\frac C2} & \tan\frac A2+\tan\frac B2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix}=0$.

Expand along the third row: the remaining $2\times2$ determinant is $\frac{1}{\cot\frac B2\cot\frac C2}-\frac{1}{\cot\frac A2\cot\frac B2}=\frac{\cot\frac A2-\cot\frac C2}{\cot\frac A2\cot\frac B2\cot\frac C2}$.
So the determinant is zero iff $\cot\frac A2=\cot\frac B2$ or $\cot\frac B2=\cot\frac C2$ or $\cot\frac C2=\cot\frac A2$.
As $\cot$ is one-one on $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$, this means $A=B$ or $B=C$ or $C=A$: the triangle is isosceles.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $p=\tan\frac A2$, $q=\tan\frac B2$, $r=\tan\frac C2$; the middle row minus $(p+q+r)\times$ the last row becomes $(-p,-q,-r)$, and the determinant is a Vandermonde-type product.
solution: The determinant is $\begin{vmatrix} \frac1p & \frac1q & \frac1r \\ q+r & r+p & p+q \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$.
Apply $R_2\to R_2-(p+q+r)R_3$: the middle row becomes $(-p,\,-q,\,-r)$.
Multiply $C_1,C_2,C_3$ by $p,q,r$: the determinant times $pqr$ equals $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ -p^2 & -q^2 & -r^2 \\ p & q & r \end{vmatrix}$.
Interchange $R_2,R_3$ (sign change): this is a Vandermonde determinant $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ p & q & r \\ p^2 & q^2 & r^2 \end{vmatrix}=(q-p)(r-p)(r-q)$ up to sign.
So the original determinant equals $\frac{(p-q)(q-r)(r-p)}{pqr}$ (verified symbolically) and vanishes iff two of $p,q,r$ are equal, i.e. two of $A,B,C$ are equal: isosceles.

useful_results: Row-sum trick: a row of the form (sum of all three) $-$ (own entry) becomes the negative of the entries after subtracting (sum) times the row of ones.
$\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ p & q & r \\ p^2 & q^2 & r^2 \end{vmatrix}=(q-p)(r-p)(r-q)$: it vanishes iff two of $p,q,r$ coincide.
In any triangle $\tan\frac A2\tan\frac B2+\tan\frac B2\tan\frac C2+\tan\frac C2\tan\frac A2=1$ and $\cot\frac A2+\cot\frac B2+\cot\frac C2=\cot\frac A2\cot\frac B2\cot\frac C2$.
A determinant that vanishes exactly when two of three angle functions are equal characterises an isosceles triangle.

concepts: Multiplication of determinants
Determinant with equal diagonal and equal off-diagonal entries
questions.question: If $ax_1^2+by_1^2+cz_1^2=ax_2^2+by_2^2+cz_2^2=ax_3^2+by_3^2+cz_3^2=d$ and $ax_2x_3+by_2y_3+cz_2z_3=ax_3x_1+by_3y_1+cz_3z_1=ax_1x_2+by_1y_2+cz_1z_2=f$, then prove that $\begin{vmatrix} x_1 & y_1 & z_1 \\ x_2 & y_2 & z_2 \\ x_3 & y_3 & z_3 \end{vmatrix}=(d-f)\left[\frac{d+2f}{abc}\right]^{1/2}$ $(a,b,c\neq0)$.
questions.key_idea: Multiply $\Delta$ by the determinant with rows $(ax_i,by_i,cz_i)$: row-by-row products give the matrix with $d$ on the diagonal and $f$ elsewhere.
solution: Let $\Delta=\begin{vmatrix} x_1 & y_1 & z_1 \\ x_2 & y_2 & z_2 \\ x_3 & y_3 & z_3 \end{vmatrix}$. Then $\begin{vmatrix} ax_1 & by_1 & cz_1 \\ ax_2 & by_2 & cz_2 \\ ax_3 & by_3 & cz_3 \end{vmatrix}=abc\,\Delta$.

So $\Delta^2=\frac{1}{abc}\begin{vmatrix} x_1 & y_1 & z_1 \\ x_2 & y_2 & z_2 \\ x_3 & y_3 & z_3 \end{vmatrix}\times\begin{vmatrix} ax_1 & by_1 & cz_1 \\ ax_2 & by_2 & cz_2 \\ ax_3 & by_3 & cz_3 \end{vmatrix}$.
Multiply row by row: the $(i,j)$ entry is $ax_ix_j+by_iy_j+cz_iz_j$, which is $d$ for $i=j$ and $f$ for $i\neq j$.
$\Delta^2=\frac{1}{abc}\begin{vmatrix} d & f & f \\ f & d & f \\ f & f & d \end{vmatrix}$.
Apply $C_1\to C_1+C_2+C_3$ and take the common factor: $\Delta^2=\frac{d+2f}{abc}\begin{vmatrix} 1 & f & f \\ 1 & d & f \\ 1 & f & d \end{vmatrix}$.
Apply $R_2\to R_2-R_1$, $R_3\to R_3-R_1$: the determinant becomes $(d-f)^2$.
So $\Delta^2=\frac{d+2f}{abc}(d-f)^2$.
Hence $\Delta=\pm(d-f)\left[\frac{d+2f}{abc}\right]^{1/2}$; the stated result is the positive sign (the sign of $\Delta$ depends on the orientation of the rows).
questions.correction_note: Two points: (i) taking the square root, the PDF writes Δ = (d−f)[(d+2f)/abc]^{1/2}, but only Δ² is determined; the sign is ± (interchanging two rows keeps d and f the same and flips Δ), so the statement holds up to sign — the ± is now stated; (ii) typo in the PDF's second determinant (third row printed 'cz3' twice; it is cz3 in row 3 and cz2 in row 2). Product, matrix of d and f, and value (d+2f)(d−f)² are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Think of the matrix of dot products as $G=(d-f)I+fJ$ ($J$ = all-ones matrix): its eigenvalues are $d-f$ (twice) and $d+2f$, so $\det G=(d+2f)(d-f)^2$ at once.
solution: With $X$ the matrix of the $x_i,y_i,z_i$ and $W=\operatorname{diag}(a,b,c)$, the matrix of the products $ax_ix_j+by_iy_j+cz_iz_j$ is $G=XWX^T$.
Hence $\det G=\Delta^2\cdot abc$.
By the given conditions $G=(d-f)I+fJ$, where $J$ is the $3\times3$ matrix of ones.
$J$ has eigenvalue $3$ on $(1,1,1)^T$ and $0$ on the 2-dimensional space orthogonal to it, so $G$ has eigenvalues $d+2f,\ d-f,\ d-f$.
Thus $abc\,\Delta^2=(d+2f)(d-f)^2$, i.e. $\Delta=\pm(d-f)\sqrt{\frac{d+2f}{abc}}$.

useful_results: $\det(A)\det(B)=\det(AB^T)$: multiplying determinants row by row turns triple products into dot products (Gram matrix).
For the $n\times n$ matrix with diagonal $d$ and off-diagonal $f$: $\det=(d+(n-1)f)(d-f)^{n-1}$.
Square-root results from $\Delta^2$ carry a $\pm$: swapping two rows leaves $d,f$ unchanged but changes the sign of $\Delta$.
A condition such as $ax_ix_j+by_iy_j+cz_iz_j=\delta_{ij}$-type (orthogonality with weights) means the rows are weighted-orthonormal and $\Delta^2abc=\det G$.

concepts: Properties and evaluation of determinants (expansion and identities)
questions.question: If $u=ax^2+2bxy+cy^2$, $u'=a'x^2+2b'xy+c'y^2$, prove that $\begin{vmatrix} y^2 & -xy & x^2 \\ a & b & c \\ a' & b' & c' \end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix} ax+by & bx+cy \\ a'x+b'y & b'x+c'y \end{vmatrix}=-\frac{1}{y}\begin{vmatrix} u & u' \\ ax+by & a'x+b'y \end{vmatrix}$.
questions.key_idea: Expand each of the three expressions and show all equal $x^2(ab'-a'b)+xy(ac'-a'c)+y^2(bc'-b'c)$.
solution: Expand the first determinant along $R_1$: $y^2(bc'-b'c)-(-xy)(ac'-a'c)+x^2(ab'-a'b)=y^2(bc'-b'c)+xy(ac'-a'c)+x^2(ab'-a'b)$.
Second determinant: $(ax+by)(b'x+c'y)-(bx+cy)(a'x+b'y)$.
Expand: $ab'x^2+ac'xy+bb'xy+bc'y^2-a'bx^2-bb'xy-a'cxy-b'cy^2$.
The $bb'xy$ terms cancel, leaving $x^2(ab'-a'b)+xy(ac'-a'c)+y^2(bc'-b'c)$: equal to the first determinant.
Third expression: $-\frac1y\left[u(a'x+b'y)-u'(ax+by)\right]$. Expand $u(a'x+b'y)=aa'x^3+ab'x^2y+2a'bx^2y+2bb'xy^2+a'cxy^2+b'cy^3$.
And $u'(ax+by)=aa'x^3+a'bx^2y+2ab'x^2y+2bb'xy^2+ac'xy^2+bc'y^3$.
Difference: $(a'b-ab')x^2y+(a'c-ac')xy^2+(b'c-bc')y^3$.
Multiplying by $-\frac1y$: $(ab'-a'b)x^2+(ac'-a'c)xy+(bc'-b'c)y^2$, which equals the first two. Hence all three are equal. $\blacksquare$

alternate_solutions.idea: Second equality by one row operation ($u=xP+yQ$, $u'=xP'+yQ'$); first equality by the Cauchy–Binet formula $\det(RS)=\sum(\text{minors of }R)(\text{minors of }S)$.
solution: Write $P=ax+by$, $Q=bx+cy$, $P'=a'x+b'y$, $Q'=b'x+c'y$. Then $u=xP+yQ$ and $u'=xP'+yQ'$ (Euler for the quadratic forms).

Third determinant: apply $R_1\to R_1-xR_2$: $\begin{vmatrix} u & u' \\ P & P' \end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix} yQ & yQ' \\ P & P' \end{vmatrix}=y(QP'-Q'P)=-y\begin{vmatrix} P & Q \\ P' & Q' \end{vmatrix}$.
So $-\frac1y\begin{vmatrix} u & u' \\ P & P' \end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix} P & Q \\ P' & Q' \end{vmatrix}$: second $=$ third.
Now $\begin{vmatrix} P & Q \\ P' & Q' \end{vmatrix}=\det(RS)$ with $R=\begin{pmatrix} a & b & c \\ a' & b' & c' \end{pmatrix}$ and $S=\begin{pmatrix} x & 0 \\ y & x \\ 0 & y \end{pmatrix}$.

Cauchy–Binet: sum over column pairs of the $2\times2$ minors of $R$ times those of $S$: the minors of $S$ are $x^2,\ xy,\ y^2$ (rows $12,13,23$) and the minors of $R$ are $ab'-a'b,\ ac'-a'c,\ bc'-b'c$.
So $\det(RS)=x^2(ab'-a'b)+xy(ac'-a'c)+y^2(bc'-b'c)$, which is the expansion of the first determinant. All three are equal.

useful_results: Euler's relation for a homogeneous quadratic $u=ax^2+2bxy+cy^2$: $u=x\,\frac{u_x}{2}+y\,\frac{u_y}{2}=x(ax+by)+y(bx+cy)$.
Cauchy–Binet: for a $2\times3$ matrix $R$ and a $3\times2$ matrix $S$, $\det(RS)=\sum_{i<j}R_{ij}S_{ij}$ (products of the matching $2\times2$ minors).
The expression $x^2(ab'-a'b)+xy(ac'-a'c)+y^2(bc'-b'c)$ is the resultant-type determinant that appears when eliminating a common root of two quadratics.
A row operation that subtracts a multiple of another row is the quickest way to simplify determinants whose entries are built from a homogeneous form.

concepts: Consistency and solution of a parametric linear system
questions.question: Test the consistency and solve them when consistent, the following system of equations for all values of $\lambda$: $x+y+z=1$, $x+3y-2z=\lambda$, $3x+(\lambda+2)y-3z=2\lambda+1$.
questions.answer: If $\lambda\neq5$: unique solution $x=\frac{\lambda+2}{3},\ y=0,\ z=\frac{1-\lambda}{3}$; if $\lambda=5$: consistent with infinitely many solutions $z=K$, $y=\frac{3K+4}{2}$, $x=-\frac{5K+2}{2}$, $K\in\mathbb{R}$
questions.key_idea: $D=3(\lambda-5)$: unique solution unless $\lambda=5$, and at $\lambda=5$ the system turns out to be consistent with a free parameter.
solution: $D=\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & -2 \\ 3 & \lambda+2 & -3 \end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & \lambda-1 & -6 \end{vmatrix}$ (by $C_2\to C_2-C_1$, $C_3\to C_3-C_1$) $=-12+3(\lambda-1)=3(\lambda-5)$.
If $\lambda\neq5$: $D\neq0$, so the system is consistent with a unique solution.
$D_1=\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ \lambda & 3 & -2 \\ 2\lambda+1 & \lambda+2 & -3 \end{vmatrix}=\lambda^2-3\lambda-10=(\lambda-5)(\lambda+2)$.
$D_2=\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & \lambda & -2 \\ 3 & 2\lambda+1 & -3 \end{vmatrix}=0$.
$D_3=\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & \lambda \\ 3 & \lambda+2 & 2\lambda+1 \end{vmatrix}=-\lambda^2+6\lambda-5=-(\lambda-1)(\lambda-5)$.
So $x=\frac{D_1}{D}=\frac{\lambda+2}{3}$, $y=0$, $z=\frac{D_3}{D}=-\frac{\lambda-1}{3}=\frac{1-\lambda}{3}$.
Check the third equation $3x+7y-3z=11$: $\frac{-15k-6+21k+28-6k}{2}=11$ ✓. So for $\lambda=5$ the system is consistent with infinitely many solutions.
questions.correction_note: Gap: the PDF states consistency at λ = 5 (D = D1 = D2 = D3 = 0) without checking it; vanishing determinants alone do not prove consistency. The check that the third equation holds is added. All determinants, solutions and the key are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate: equation 2 $-$ equation 1 and equation 3 $-\,3\times$ equation 1 give two equations in $y,z$ whose difference is $(\lambda-5)y=0$.
solution: Equation 2 $-$ equation 1: $2y-3z=\lambda-1$ (A). Equation 3 $-\,3\times$ equation 1: $(\lambda-1)y-6z=2\lambda-2$ (B).
Multiply (A) by $2$: $4y-6z=2(\lambda-1)$. Subtract from (B): $(\lambda-5)y=0$.
If $\lambda\neq5$: $y=0$, then $z=\frac{1-\lambda}{3}$ from (A) and $x=1-y-z=\frac{\lambda+2}{3}$: a unique solution.
If $\lambda=5$: (A) and (B) are the same equation $2y-3z=4$, so the system reduces to two independent equations and is consistent.
With $z=k$: $y=\frac{3k+4}{2}$, $x=1-y-k=-\frac{5k+2}{2}$: infinitely many solutions.

useful_results: Subtract equations to expose $(\text{parameter}-\text{critical value})\cdot(\text{unknown})=0$; that factor tells where the system changes character.
$D=D_1=D_2=D_3=0$ does not by itself prove consistency; reduce by elimination (or compare ranks) to confirm.
Column operations $C_j\to C_j-C_1$ make a row $(1,0,0)$ and reduce a $3\times3$ determinant to $2\times2$.
Here $D_2=0$ for every $\lambda$ because the second column of the numerator matrix is proportional to the first: $y=0$ always.

concepts: Properties of determinants (conjugate, transpose) and Hermitian matrices
questions.question: Prove that the value of the determinant $\begin{vmatrix} -7 & 5+3i & \frac23-4i \\ 5-3i & 8 & 4+5i \\ \frac23+4i & 4-5i & 9 \end{vmatrix}$ is real.
questions.key_idea: The conjugate of this matrix equals its transpose, and a determinant equals the determinant of its transpose.
solution: Let $A$ be the given matrix and $\bar A$ the matrix of conjugates of its entries.
$\bar A=\begin{pmatrix} -7 & 5-3i & \frac23+4i \\ 5+3i & 8 & 4-5i \\ \frac23-4i & 4+5i & 9 \end{pmatrix}=A^T$.
Hence $|\bar A|=|A^T|=|A|$.
The determinant is a polynomial in the entries with integer coefficients, so $|\bar A|=\overline{|A|}$.
Therefore $\overline{|A|}=|A|$, i.e. $|A|$ is real. $\blacksquare$

alternate_solutions.idea: Expand by Sarrus' rule: for a Hermitian matrix every term either is real or pairs with its conjugate.
solution: Write $A=(a_{ij})$ with $a_{ji}=\overline{a_{ij}}$ and real diagonal entries $a_{11},a_{22},a_{33}$.

Since $a_{21}=\bar a_{12}$, $a_{32}=\bar a_{23}$, $a_{31}=\bar a_{13}$: $a_{13}a_{21}a_{32}=\overline{a_{31}a_{12}a_{23}}$, so the two middle terms add up to $2\operatorname{Re}(a_{12}a_{23}a_{31})$, a real number.
The last three terms are $-a_{22}|a_{13}|^2-a_{11}|a_{23}|^2-a_{33}|a_{12}|^2$, all real.

useful_results: A square matrix with $\bar A=A^T$ is Hermitian; its determinant is real and its eigenvalues are real.
For any square matrix $\det(\bar A)=\overline{\det A}$ and $\det(A^T)=\det A$.
For a skew-Hermitian matrix of odd order $n$, $\overline{\det A}=(-1)^n\det A$, so the determinant is purely imaginary.

concepts: Evaluation of a determinant by column operations
questions.question: Prove that $\begin{vmatrix} 1+a^2-b^2 & 2ab & -2b \\ 2ab & 1-a^2+b^2 & 2a \\ 2b & -2a & 1-a^2-b^2 \end{vmatrix}=(1+a^2+b^2)^3$.
questions.key_idea: $C_1\to C_1-bC_3$ and $C_2\to C_2+aC_3$ create zeros and the common factor $1+a^2+b^2$.
solution: Apply $C_1\to C_1-bC_3$ and $C_2\to C_2+aC_3$.
First column: $\left(1+a^2-b^2+2b^2,\ 2ab-2ab,\ 2b-b(1-a^2-b^2)\right)=\left(1+a^2+b^2,\ 0,\ b(1+a^2+b^2)\right)$.
Second column: $\left(2ab-2ab,\ 1-a^2+b^2+2a^2,\ -2a+a(1-a^2-b^2)\right)=\left(0,\ 1+a^2+b^2,\ -a(1+a^2+b^2)\right)$.
So the determinant is $\begin{vmatrix} 1+a^2+b^2 & 0 & -2b \\ 0 & 1+a^2+b^2 & 2a \\ b(1+a^2+b^2) & -a(1+a^2+b^2) & 1-a^2-b^2 \end{vmatrix}$.
Take $(1+a^2+b^2)$ out of $C_1$ and of $C_2$: $(1+a^2+b^2)^2\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & -2b \\ 0 & 1 & 2a \\ b & -a & 1-a^2-b^2 \end{vmatrix}$.
So the determinant equals $(1+a^2+b^2)^3$. $\blacksquare$

alternate_solutions.idea: Each row has the same length $1+a^2+b^2$ and different rows are orthogonal, so $MM^T=(1+a^2+b^2)^2I$, which gives $\det M=\pm(1+a^2+b^2)^3$; continuity fixes the sign.
solution: Let $s=1+a^2+b^2$. Row 1 times row 1: $(1+a^2-b^2)^2+4a^2b^2+4b^2=s^2$; similarly rows 2 and 3 have squared length $s^2$.
So $MM^T=s^2I$ (this is the Euler–Rodrigues form of a rotation scaled by $s$).
Therefore $(\det M)^2=s^6$, so $\det M=\pm s^3$.
$\det M$ is continuous in $(a,b)$ and never $0$ (as $s\ge1$); at $a=b=0$, $M=I$ and $\det M=1>0$. So $\det M=+s^3=(1+a^2+b^2)^3$.

useful_results: If the rows of an $n\times n$ matrix are pairwise orthogonal with equal length $\ell$, then $MM^T=\ell^2I$ and $\det M=\pm\ell^n$.
Euler–Rodrigues: $(1-|\mathbf n|^2)I+2\mathbf n\mathbf n^T-2[\mathbf n]_\times$ is $(1+|\mathbf n|^2)$ times a rotation; here $\mathbf n=(a,b,0)$.
To make a $3\times3$ determinant of this type collapse, subtract multiples of the column with the simplest entries ($C_3$ here) from the others.
Check at $a=b=0$: $\det I=1=(1)^3$; at $a=1,b=0$: the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}2&0&0\\0&0&2\\0&-2&0\end{pmatrix}$ with $\det=8=2^3$.

concepts: Properties of determinants (permutation expansion)
Tangent of a sum and the identity tan X + tan Y + tan Z = tan X tan Y tan Z
questions.question: Show that the value of the determinant $\begin{vmatrix} \tan(A+P) & \tan(B+P) & \tan(C+P) \\ \tan(A+Q) & \tan(B+Q) & \tan(C+Q) \\ \tan(A+R) & \tan(B+R) & \tan(C+R) \end{vmatrix}$ vanishes for all values of $A,B,C,P,Q$ and $R$ where $A+B+C+P+Q+R=0$.
questions.key_idea: Every product in the expansion has arguments summing to $0$, so each product of three tangents equals their sum, and the sums cancel in pairs.
solution: If $X+Y+Z=0$ then $\tan X+\tan Y+\tan Z=\tan X\tan Y\tan Z$ (since $\tan(X+Y)=-\tan Z$).

Expand along $R_1$: $\tan(A+P)\left[\tan(B+Q)\tan(C+R)-\tan(B+R)\tan(C+Q)\right]-\tan(B+P)\left[\tan(A+Q)\tan(C+R)-\tan(A+R)\tan(C+Q)\right]+\tan(C+P)\left[\tan(A+Q)\tan(B+R)-\tan(A+R)\tan(B+Q)\right]$.
Each of the six products of three entries uses each of $A,B,C,P,Q,R$ exactly once, so its three arguments add up to $A+B+C+P+Q+R=0$.
Apply the identity to each product: e.g. $\tan(A+P)\tan(B+Q)\tan(C+R)=\tan(A+P)+\tan(B+Q)+\tan(C+R)$.

The signed sum is $\left[t_{AP}+t_{BQ}+t_{CR}\right]-\left[t_{AP}+t_{BR}+t_{CQ}\right]-\left[t_{BP}+t_{AQ}+t_{CR}\right]+\left[t_{BP}+t_{AR}+t_{CQ}\right]+\left[t_{CP}+t_{AQ}+t_{BR}\right]-\left[t_{CP}+t_{AR}+t_{BQ}\right]$ where $t_{AP}=\tan(A+P)$ etc.
Every term occurs once with $+$ and once with $-$, so the sum is $0$.
Hence the determinant vanishes for all such $A,B,C,P,Q,R$. $\blacksquare$
questions.correction_note: The PDF only quotes the identity tan X + tan Y + tan Z = tan X tan Y tan Z and writes out the expansion by R1, ending with '= 0' without showing why it is zero. The reason (each of the six products has argument sum 0, so equals the sum of its three tangents, and the six sums cancel in pairs) was written out; also checked numerically.

alternate_solutions.idea: Replace each product by the sum of its three entries and regroup by entry: each entry $t_{ij}$ is then multiplied by the sum of the signs of the two permutations that use it, and these signs cancel.
solution: Write the determinant as $\sum_\sigma\operatorname{sgn}\sigma\,t_{1\sigma(1)}t_{2\sigma(2)}t_{3\sigma(3)}$ over the six permutations of the columns.
In every term the three arguments are the six angles used once each, so they add to $0$ and the product equals $t_{1\sigma(1)}+t_{2\sigma(2)}+t_{3\sigma(3)}$.
Hence $\det=\sum_\sigma\operatorname{sgn}\sigma\sum_{i}t_{i\sigma(i)}=\sum_{i,j}t_{ij}\left(\sum_{\sigma:\,\sigma(i)=j}\operatorname{sgn}\sigma\right)$.
For fixed $(i,j)$ exactly two permutations of three symbols send $i$ to $j$; they differ by one transposition, so their signs are opposite and the inner sum is $0$.
Therefore $\det=0$.

useful_results: If $X+Y+Z=n\pi$ then $\tan X+\tan Y+\tan Z=\tan X\tan Y\tan Z$; similarly, if $A+B+C=\frac\pi2$ then $\tan A\tan B+\tan B\tan C+\tan C\tan A=1$.
The same argument shows $\det[f(\theta_j+\varphi_i)]=0$ for any function $f$ with $f(X)f(Y)f(Z)=f(X)+f(Y)+f(Z)$ whenever $X+Y+Z=0$ and $\sum\theta_j+\sum\varphi_i=0$.
For $n=3$ the two permutations through a fixed entry have opposite signs, which is why 'product $=$ sum' kills a $3\times3$ determinant.
Numerical check: $A=0.3,B=-0.5,C=0.8,P=0.2,Q=-0.6$, $R=-0.2$ gives a determinant of order $10^{-15}$.

concepts: Factorisation of a Vandermonde-type determinant
questions.paragraph: Let $x,y,z\in\mathbb{R}^+$ and $\Delta=\begin{vmatrix} x & x^3 & x^4-1 \\ y & y^3 & y^4-1 \\ z & z^3 & z^4-1 \end{vmatrix}$.
questions.question: If $x\neq y\neq z$ and $x,y,z$ are in G.P. and $\Delta=0$ then $y$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Split the last column and factor out the Vandermonde product: $\Delta=V\left[xyz(xy+yz+zx)-(x+y+z)\right]$; a G.P. substitution then forces $y^4=1$.
solution: Split the last column: $\Delta=\begin{vmatrix} x & x^3 & x^4 \\ y & y^3 & y^4 \\ z & z^3 & z^4 \end{vmatrix}-\begin{vmatrix} x & x^3 & 1 \\ y & y^3 & 1 \\ z & z^3 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$.
Take $x,y,z$ out of the rows of the first determinant: it equals $xyz\begin{vmatrix} 1 & x^2 & x^3 \\ 1 & y^2 & y^3 \\ 1 & z^2 & z^3 \end{vmatrix}$.

Let $V=\begin{vmatrix} 1 & x & x^2 \\ 1 & y & y^2 \\ 1 & z & z^2 \end{vmatrix}=(y-x)(z-x)(z-y)$. Standard results: $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & x^2 & x^3 \\ 1 & y^2 & y^3 \\ 1 & z^2 & z^3 \end{vmatrix}=V(xy+yz+zx)$ and $\begin{vmatrix} x & x^3 & 1 \\ y & y^3 & 1 \\ z & z^3 & 1 \end{vmatrix}=V(x+y+z)$.
Hence $\Delta=V\left[xyz(xy+yz+zx)-(x+y+z)\right]$.
As $x,y,z$ are distinct, $V\neq0$, so $\Delta=0$ means $xyz(xy+yz+zx)=x+y+z$.
G.P.: put $x=\frac{y}{r}$, $z=yr$. Then $xyz=y^3$, $xy+yz+zx=y^2\left(\frac1r+r+1\right)$ and $x+y+z=y\left(\frac1r+1+r\right)$.
The condition becomes $y^5\left(r+1+\frac1r\right)=y\left(r+1+\frac1r\right)$, i.e. $y\left(y^4-1\right)\left(r+1+\frac1r\right)=0$.
Since $y>0$ and $r+1+\frac1r>0$, we get $y^4=1$, so $y=1$. Answer (A).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's solution is only 'put x = y/r, z = yr ⇒ y = 1'; the factorisation of Δ and the algebra leading to y⁴ = 1 are missing and were written out. Answer (A) is correct.
useful_results: Generalised Vandermonde determinants: with $V=(y-x)(z-x)(z-y)$, the determinant with columns $1,x^2,x^3$ equals $V\,e_2$ and the one with columns $1,x,x^3$ equals $V\,e_1$ ($e_1=x+y+z$, $e_2=xy+yz+zx$): gaps in the exponents give elementary symmetric functions (Schur pattern).
A determinant that vanishes when two variables are equal is divisible by $(x-y)(y-z)(z-x)$.
Parametrise a G.P. as $\left(\frac yr,\,y,\,yr\right)$ and an A.P. as $(y-d,\,y,\,y+d)$: the middle term then factors out of symmetric expressions.
Check: $y=1$, $r=2$: $x=\frac12$, $z=2$: $xyz=1$, $xy+yz+zx=\frac12+2+1=\frac72$ and $x+y+z=\frac72$ ✓.

concepts: Vieta's formulas and AM–GM inequality for roots of a cubic
Determinant with two equal rows
questions.paragraph: Let $x,y,z\in\mathbb{R}^+$ and $\Delta=\begin{vmatrix} x & x^3 & x^4-1 \\ y & y^3 & y^4-1 \\ z & z^3 & z^4-1 \end{vmatrix}$.
questions.question: If $x,y,z$ are roots of $t^3-21t^2+bt-343=0$, $b\in\mathbb{R}$, then $\Delta=$
questions.key_idea: Sum $21$ and product $343=7^3$ give equality in AM–GM, so $x=y=z=7$ and $\Delta$ has equal rows.
solution: By Vieta: $x+y+z=21$ and $xyz=343$ (with $x,y,z\in\mathbb{R}^+$).
AM–GM: $\frac{x+y+z}{3}=7$ and $(xyz)^{1/3}=7$, so $\frac{x+y+z}{3}=(xyz)^{1/3}$: equality holds.
Equality in AM–GM happens only when $x=y=z$; hence $x=y=z=7$.
Then the rows of $\Delta$ are identical, so $\Delta=0$. Answer (B).
(The PDF's route: take $x=\frac yr$, $z=yr$; $xyz=y^3=343\Rightarrow y=7$ and $\frac7r+7+7r=21\Rightarrow r=1$, again $x=y=z=7$. That substitution assumes a G.P., which AM–GM does not need.)
questions.correction_note: The PDF substitutes x = y/r, z = yr, i.e. it assumes the roots are in G.P., which is not given for a general cubic; the conclusion x = y = z = 7 is right but needs AM–GM (sum 21, product 343) as the justification. Replaced by the AM–GM argument; answer (B) unchanged.
useful_results: If a set of positive numbers has $\frac{\text{sum}}{n}=(\text{product})^{1/n}$ then all the numbers are equal.
Vieta for $t^3-pt^2+qt-r$: $e_1=p$, $e_2=q$, $e_3=r$; here $p=21$, $r=343$ force the roots $7,7,7$ and then $b=147$.
A determinant with two equal rows (or columns) is $0$; this is the quickest way to recognise $\Delta=0$ once $x=y=z$.
Conversely, for positive roots with $e_1=21$ and $e_3=343$ the cubic must be $(t-7)^3$, so $b$ is forced to be $147$.

questions.paragraph: Let $x,y,z\in\mathbb{R}^+$ and $\Delta=\begin{vmatrix} x & x^3 & x^4-1 \\ y & y^3 & y^4-1 \\ z & z^3 & z^4-1 \end{vmatrix}$.
questions.question: If $x,y,z$ are in A.P. and $\Delta=0$ then $2xy^2z+x^2z^2=$
questions.key_idea: Using $\Delta=V\left[xyz(xy+yz+zx)-(x+y+z)\right]$ with $2y=x+z$, the vanishing factor becomes $xz(2y^2+xz)=3$.
solution: From Q17: $\Delta=V\left[xyz(xy+yz+zx)-(x+y+z)\right]$ with $V=(y-x)(z-x)(z-y)$. Take $x,y,z$ distinct (as in Q17), so $V\neq0$.
Then $\Delta=0$ gives $xyz(xy+yz+zx)=x+y+z$.
A.P.: $2y=x+z$, so $x+y+z=3y$ and $xy+yz+zx=y(x+z)+zx=2y^2+xz$.
The condition becomes $y\cdot xz\,(2y^2+xz)=3y$.
Since $y>0$: $xz\,(2y^2+xz)=3$, i.e. $2xy^2z+x^2z^2=3$. Answer (C).

The value 3 is forced only for distinct x, y, z (as in Q17); then Δ = 0 gives xyz(xy+yz+zx) = x+y+z and hence xz(2y²+xz) = 3. Answer (C) kept; the question should state x ≠ y ≠ z.
useful_results: For distinct $x,y,z$: $\Delta=0\iff xyz(xy+yz+zx)=x+y+z$ (the determinant of this paragraph).
In an A.P. $2y=x+z$: $x+y+z=3y$ and $xy+yz+zx=2y^2+xz$; in a G.P. $y^2=xz$.
Always check the degenerate case $x=y=z=t$: then $\Delta=0$ trivially for every $t$, so it cannot determine a unique value.
Numerical example with distinct terms: $y=1.3$, $x=0.320172\ldots$, $z=2.279827\ldots$ gives $\Delta=0$ and $2xy^2z+x^2z^2=3$.

questions.paragraph: Consider the system of equations $2x+ay+6z=8$, $x+2y+bz=5$ and $x+y+3z=4$. Then:
questions.question: The system of equations will have infinite solutions if:
questions.key_idea: Infinitely many solutions need $D=D_1=D_2=D_3=0$; $D_3=a-2$ forces $a=2$, and then the first equation is twice the third.
solution: For infinitely many solutions $D=D_1=D_2=D_3=0$. $D_3=0$ gives $a=2$; then $D=D_1=0$ and $D_2=0$ hold for every $b$.

Check: for $a=2$ the first equation is $2x+2y+6z=8$, i.e. $2\times$ the third equation, so only two independent equations remain in three unknowns, and they are consistent: infinitely many solutions for every $b$.
Hence the condition is $a=2$ (option D); $b=3$ alone ($a\neq2$) gives no solution, and $b=2$ or $a=3$ give a unique solution.

alternate_solutions.idea: Compute $E_1-2E_3$: it removes $x$ and $z$ at once and leaves $(a-2)y=0$.
solution: First equation minus twice the third: $(2x+ay+6z)-2(x+y+3z)=(a-2)y$, and the right side is $8-2\cdot4=0$, so $(a-2)y=0$.
If $a=2$ this is $0=0$: the first equation is a multiple of the third, so two independent equations $x+y+3z=4$, $x+2y+bz=5$ remain: infinitely many solutions for every $b$.
If $a\neq2$ then $y=0$ and the other two give $x+3z=4$, $x+bz=5$, so $(b-3)z=1$: a unique solution when $b\neq3$ and none when $b=3$.
So infinitely many solutions occur exactly for $a=2$ (option D).

useful_results: Subtract a multiple of one equation from another to remove two unknowns at once: $E_1-2E_3$ here gives $(a-2)y=0$, so $a=2$ is the critical value.
Summary for a $3\times3$ system: $D\neq0$ unique; $D=0$ and some $D_i\neq0$ none; $D=D_i=0$ requires a rank check (infinite or none).

concepts: Cramer's rule and consistency of a parametric linear system
questions.paragraph: Consider the system of equations $2x+ay+6z=8$, $x+2y+bz=5$ and $x+y+3z=4$. Then:
questions.question: The given system of equations will have a unique solution if:
questions.key_idea: A unique solution needs $D=(a-2)(b-3)\neq0$.
solution: For a unique solution $D\neq0$, i.e. $(a-2)(b-3)\neq0$.
Hence $a\neq2$ and $b\neq3$ (option A).
Then $x,y,z$ are determined by Cramer's rule: $y=\frac{D_2}{D}=0$ and $z=\frac{D_3}{D}=\frac{a-2}{(a-2)(b-3)}=\frac1{b-3}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate to $(a-2)y=0$ and $(b-3)z=1$: both can be solved uniquely exactly when $a\neq2$ and $b\neq3$.
solution: Then $E_2-E_3$ gives $y+(b-3)z=1$.
For $a\neq2$: $y=0$, so $(b-3)z=1$; this has a unique $z=\frac1{b-3}$ iff $b\neq3$.
Then $x=4-y-3z=4-\frac{3}{b-3}$ is unique. Hence a unique solution iff $a\neq2$ and $b\neq3$ (option A).

useful_results: Unique solution $\iff\det A\neq0$; here the determinant factorises into independent conditions on $a$ and $b$.
Under the unique solution: $y=0$, $z=\frac{1}{b-3}$, $x=4-\frac{3}{b-3}$ (check $a=3,b=4$: $x=1$, $y=0$, $z=1$: $2+0+6=8$ ✓).
A determinant that factorises into $(\text{param}_1-c_1)(\text{param}_2-c_2)$ gives independent exclusions.
Check $a=3,b=4$: $D=1\cdot1=1\neq0$ ✓.

questions.question: The domain of the function $f(x)$:
questions.key_idea: The determinant reduces to $150+100\sin2x$, defined for every real $x$.
solution: Apply $R_2\to R_2-R_1$ and $R_3\to R_3-R_1$: $f(x)=\begin{vmatrix} 5+\sin^2x & \cos^2x & 4\sin2x \\ -5 & 5 & 0 \\ -5 & 0 & 5 \end{vmatrix}$.
Equivalently $f(x)=5\left(5\cos^2x\right)+5\left(25+5\sin^2x+20\sin2x\right)$ (the PDF's grouping).
This expression is defined for all real $x$, so the domain is $\mathbb{R}=(-\infty,\infty)$. Answer (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Every entry is a polynomial in $\sin x,\cos x$, so $f(x)$ is defined for every real $x$ before any computation; the closed form $150+100\sin 2x$ then confirms it.
solution: All nine entries $5+\sin^2x$, $\cos^2x$, $4\sin2x$, $\sin^2x$, $5+\cos^2x$, $5+4\sin2x$ are defined for every real $x$.
A $3\times3$ determinant is a polynomial in its entries, so it is defined for every real $x$: the domain is $\mathbb{R}$.
(Closed form via row sums: each row sums to $6+4\sin2x$; $C_1\to C_1+C_2+C_3$ and then $R_2-R_1$, $R_3-R_1$ give $f(x)=25(6+4\sin2x)=150+100\sin2x$, again defined for all $x$.)
Hence the domain is $(-\infty,\infty)$ (option B).

useful_results: The domain of a determinant function is the intersection of the domains of its entries; entries built from $\sin,\cos$ and polynomials are defined everywhere.
Row-sum trick: if all rows sum to the same $S$, then $C_1\to C_1+C_2+C_3$ gives $S$ times a determinant with first column of ones.
Here every row sums to $6+4\sin2x$, which gives $f(x)=25(6+4\sin 2x)$ directly.
Periodicity: $f$ has period $\pi$ because $\sin2x$ does.

questions.question: The range of the function $f(x)$:
questions.key_idea: The determinant is $150+100\sin2x$, so its range is $[150-100,\,150+100]$.
solution: Apply $R_2\to R_2-R_1$ and $R_3\to R_3-R_1$: $f(x)=\begin{vmatrix} 5+\sin^2x & \cos^2x & 4\sin2x \\ -5 & 5 & 0 \\ -5 & 0 & 5 \end{vmatrix}$.
Equivalently $f(x)=5\left(5\cos^2x\right)+5\left(25+5\sin^2x+20\sin2x\right)$ (the PDF's grouping).
So the range is $[50,250]$ (option A).

alternate_solutions.idea: All three rows have the same sum $6+4\sin2x$, so $C_1\to C_1+C_2+C_3$ makes the first column $S=6+4\sin2x$ everywhere and $f=25S$.
solution: Row sums: $(5+\sin^2x)+\cos^2x+4\sin2x=6+4\sin2x$; $\sin^2x+(5+\cos^2x)+4\sin2x=6+4\sin2x$; $\sin^2x+\cos^2x+(5+4\sin2x)=6+4\sin2x$.
Apply $C_1\to C_1+C_2+C_3$ and take $S=6+4\sin2x$ out of the first column: $f(x)=S\begin{vmatrix} 1 & \cos^2x & 4\sin2x \\ 1 & 5+\cos^2x & 4\sin2x \\ 1 & \cos^2x & 5+4\sin2x \end{vmatrix}$.
Apply $R_2\to R_2-R_1$, $R_3\to R_3-R_1$: the determinant becomes $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & \cos^2x & 4\sin2x \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{vmatrix}=25$.

useful_results: The range of $a+b\sin(kx+c)$ is $[a-|b|,\,a+|b|]$; here $a=150$, $b=100$.
If every row (or column) of a determinant has the same sum $S$, then $S$ is a factor (add all columns to the first).
Pattern: after $R_2-R_1$, $R_3-R_1$ a block of the form $5I$ appears; the determinant is then $25$ times the remaining pivot.
Check: $x=\frac\pi4$ gives $f=250$ and $x=-\frac\pi4$ gives $f=50$ (maximum and minimum attained).
